description: I’m a MIIGAiK student interested in geodesy, remote sensing, and geospatial data analysis. I’m participating solo in Dancing with the SARs to explore how satellite radar can help us understand changes on Earth’s surface.
summary:
We developed an interactive map showing how the shoreline of Germany's Forggensee reservoir changed between April and July 2026 using NASA's NISAR radar data.

Our approach combines HH, HV and VV polarizations to identify water boundaries and measure shoreline displacement along 46 fixed transects. At our highlighted location, T35, radar indicates a 1.31 km shift, consistent with a separate check using Sentinel-2 imagery, water-level records and terrain data. Across all 11 transects with usable complete checks, the mean absolute discrepancy is 88 m.

The viewer lets users explore radar channels, compare dates and inspect the evidence behind each measurement. Radar provides the shoreline estimates; optical imagery and other observations provide the checks.

Addressing Dancing with the SARs, the project makes complex radar observations understandable through clear maps and graphs. It demonstrates an exploratory approach to monitoring seasonal reservoir changes and identifying locations that need closer observation.
details:
Forggensee is a managed reservoir on the River Lech in Bavaria, Germany. Seasonal drawdown and refill move its shoreline across shallow terrain. Our project uses NASA's NISAR radar observations to map this change and make the results understandable through an interactive viewer, maps and graphs.

HOW IT WORKS

We analyse NISAR L2 GCOV data acquired on 6 April and 23 July 2026, using HH, HV and VV polarization channels on a 20 m grid.

For April, water classification combines local thresholds with agreement between at least two of the three channels. For July, a Random Forest classifier uses the three channels and two channel log-ratios, trained on automatically selected SAR examples. This hybrid approach was selected after comparing alternative methods on the study area.

We extract water boundaries and measure displacement along 46 fixed transects crossing the shoreline. Sentinel-2 imagery, reservoir water-level records and terrain data provide a separate check, accounting approximately for water-level differences between radar and optical acquisition dates. Optical imagery is not used to trace the SAR boundaries or supply classifier training labels.

RESULTS

At the highlighted transect T35, SAR indicates a shoreline displacement of 1,310 m, consistent with an approximate optical, water-level and terrain check of 1,285–1,324 m.

Across the study area, 43 of 46 transects yield a nominal displacement estimate. Eleven have usable complete checks, with a mean absolute discrepancy of 88 m. All usable checks are included in this statistic. A more difficult case, T24, is documented in the appendix and interactive viewer.

WHAT USERS CAN EXPLORE

The viewer allows users to switch between the water-change map, radar dates and polarization channels, inspect individual transects, and compare the radar results with optical imagery. Clear graphics connect each measurement to its location and supporting evidence.

The project package includes the interactive viewer, an A2 map, an editable QGIS project, measurement tables, source-data subsets, analysis code and a presentation.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

The project demonstrates how radar observations can support seasonal reservoir monitoring and help identify locations for closer inspection. Its main contribution is connecting radar-derived boundaries, measurable shoreline movement and supporting checks in one accessible visual workflow.

We considered radar speckle, differences between polarization channels, shallow terrain, acquisition-date mismatches and sensitivity to processing choices. This is an exploratory comparison on one reservoir and two dates; robustness and performance on new sites or dates require further testing.

TOOLS

Python, GDAL, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-image, scikit-learn, Matplotlib, QGIS, HTML and JavaScript were used for processing, analysis and visualisation. Presentation materials were produced with python-pptx and ReportLab. OpenAI Codex assisted with code, processing experiments, interpretation drafts, graphics, translation and documentation.
